U.S. consumer prices rose 0.9% in March 2026, putting the annual inflation rate at 3.3%, the highest since May 2024, largely driven by a 21.2% surge in gasoline prices. Core CPI, excluding food and energy, rose 0.2% monthly and 2.6% year-over-year. The data indicates significant upward pressure from energy costs due to geopolitical conflict. Key Inflation Metrics (March 2026) Annual CPI (Headline): 3.3% Monthly CPI (Headline): 0.9% Core CPI (Annual): 2.6% Core CPI (Monthly): 0.2% Energy Prices: +10.9% monthly Key Details on Inflation Gasoline Surge: Gasoline prices recorded a 21.2% monthly jump, the largest since data collection began in 1967, contributing nearly 75% of the total monthly rise. Energy Impact: While energy makes up roughly 7% of the CPI basket, its overall economic impact is closer to 15% due to its influence on other goods. Core Inflation: Core CPI, which is often considered a better measure of underlying inflation, was slightly below expectations at 2.6% annually. Market Impact: The high inflation reading led to a dip in consumer sentiment, reaching the lowest level in the history of the University of Michigan survey. Upcoming Changes: The CPI for April 2026 is scheduled to be released on May 12, 2026, with several CPI series being rebased to December 2024=100. How the CPI is Calculated The CPI is calculated by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) and measures the average change over time in prices paid by consumers for a market basket of goods and services. Formula: The percentage change in the CPI from one period to another represents the inflation rate. Types: There are two main types of CPI calculated by the BLS: CPI-U: Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (most common). CPI-W: Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers. Inflation Impact on Wages The CPI is often used to adjust wages, salaries, and pensions for inflation. The CPI-W, for instance, is used to calculate the cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs) for Social Security recipients.
